papers.title: Quality of life after conservative versus elective surgical management of first-episode uncomplicated diverticulitis: a single-center prospective study
papers.authors: Quero G, Langellotti L, Tortorelli A, Tondolo V, Biffoni B, Daloiso G
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Optimal long-term management after a first episode of uncomplicated acute diverticulitis (AD) remains debated. Quality of life (QoL) is increasingly recognized as a key outcome to guide individualized decision-making between clinical surveillance and elective sigmoid resection.
METHODS: This single-center prospective longitudinal observational study enrolled adults with a first episode of uncomplicated AD (Hinchey 0-1a). After recovery from the index episode, patients underwent either clinical follow-up (nonsurgery group) or elective laparoscopic sigmoidectomy (surgery group) according to routine clinical decision-making. Diverticulitis-specific QoL was assessed using the DV-QoL questionnaire, retrospectively referring to the month before the index episode and prospectively at 1, 6, and 12 months after post-episode management. The primary aim was to describe and compare DV-QoL trajectories between groups. A DV-QoL score ≥ 3.2 was used to define a non-acceptable symptom state (Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS) threshold). Predictors of non-acceptable QoL were explored in conservatively managed patients.
RESULTS: A total of 137 patients were included: 96 (70%) in the nonsurgery group and 41 (30%) in the surgery group. Baseline characteristics were comparable. Pre-episode DV-QoL scores were similar between groups (0.19 ± 0.29 versus 0.12 ± 0.33; p = 0.14). DV-QoL total scores were significantly higher (worse QoL) in the nonsurgery group at 1 month (2.60 ± 2.70 versus 0.11 ± 0.15; p < 0.001), 6 months (2.09 ± 2.24 versus 0.05 ± 0.12; p < 0.001), and 12 months (1.92 ± 2.07 versus 0.02 ± 0.07; p < 0.001). Non-acceptable QoL (PASS ≥ 3.2) occurred only in the non-surgery cohort at all timepoints, whereas no surgical patient exceeded PASS. Younger age independently predicted non-acceptable QoL in conservatively managed patients.
CONCLUSIONS: Elective laparoscopic sigmoidectomy after a first uncomplicated AD episode was associated with sustained improvements in disease-specific QoL compared with clinical follow-up. Routine DV-QoL assessment may help identify patients at risk of persistent impairment and optimize individualized surgical decision-making.

papers.title: Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals pro-tumorigenic intestinal mast cell programs in colorectal cancer
papers.authors: Putro E, Carnevale A, Marangio C, Pietropaolo G, Milito N, Peruzzi G
papers.abstract: Mast cells (MCs) are multifunctional immune cells with context-dependent functions in cancer. In colorectal cancer (CRC), their contribution remains debated, suggesting that distinct MC subsets may either support tumor progression or promote anti-tumor immunity. Using single-cell RNA sequencing in a mouse model of inflammation-driven CRC, we uncovered extensive MC plasticity during tumor progression. Transcriptomic profiling and pseudotime trajectory analysis revealed a transition from precursor-like MCs exclusively present in adjacent tissue to differentiated tumor-associated MC (TAMC) subsets. TAMCs displayed a distinct repertoire of proteases and pro-inflammatory cytokines, contributing to increased vascular permeability and recruitment of additional immune cells. Moreover, TAMCs exhibited upregulation of molecules with immunosuppressive potential and underwent a tumor microenvironment (TME)-driven metabolic reprogramming. Accordingly, antibody-mediated MC depletion reduced tumor burden. Notably, most of the transcriptional features identified in a murine CRC model were recapitulated in human CRC, supporting the translational relevance of this MC program. Our findings identify a tumor-adapted MC state that orchestrates immune evasion and tissue remodeling during CRC progression, supporting the notion that MC are reprogrammed toward an immune-suppressive and pro-tumorigenic phenotype.

papers.title: Glutaredoxin 1 facilitates colitis recovery by controlling glutathionylation and activity of STAT6 in M2 macrophages
papers.authors: Guo L, Lei Y, Wang T, Gu L, Shen L, Liu Q
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is characterized by oxidative stress and intractable inflammation. Current therapeutic strategies are far from satisfactory because of its not fully understood pathogenesis. M2 macrophages can promote inflammation resolution and tissue repair, and are attractive therapeutic targets of IBD. However, the intrinsic nature of redox regulation of M2 macrophages in IBD is still elusive. DSS-induced murine colitis recovery model and GEO data suggest that glutaredoxin 1 (Grx1) might be the main redox modulator of macrophages in IBD. Grx1 is the main enzyme negatively catalyzing ROS-elicited protein glutathionylation. Depletion of Grx1 delays colitis recovery, while recombinant Grx1 protein treatment benefits colitis recovery, with decreased glutathionylation and increased M2 macrophages. Grx1-deficient IL-4-polarized macrophages show reduced pro-repair effects on injured intestinal epithelial tight junctions, impaired efferocytosis, and compromised maintenance of the M2-polarized state. Mechanistically, STAT6, a pivotal transcription factor in M2 macrophages, is proved to be the main target of Grx1 and glutathionylation. Grx1 disruption decreases nuclear translocation of STAT6 in macrophages, while mutation of modified cysteine in STAT6 displays reverse effect. Finally, Grx1-STAT6 signaling is verified in colitis recovery models. Our results reveal Grx1/glutathionylation as crucial negative redox regulatory mechanisms of M2 macrophages in IBD, which exhibits promising therapeutic potential of IBD.

papers.title: Proposed Interactions and Crosstalk Among Biological Aging Biomarkers (Telomere Length, Telomerase, Sirtuins, mtDNA Copy Number and mtDNA Methylation Levels) and Their Potential Role in Colorectal Cancer Risk: A Review
papers.authors: Macamo E, Naidoo P, Senzani S, Bhengu K, Kader S, Mkhize-Kwitshana Z
papers.abstract: There is a rapid increase in early onset CRC worldwide. This incidence is profoundly influenced by biological aging in the colon, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely defined. This review critically evaluates evidence supporting proposed interactions among telomere dynamics, sirtuins, and mitochondrial biomarkers during colon aging and as CRC risk predictors, while highlighting areas where mechanistic validation remains limited. This insight paves the way for novel early-detection biomarkers, personalized preventive approaches, and treatments designed to directly interfere with aging mechanisms and CRC risk.

papers.title: Colorectal Cancer Biomarkers: The Expanding Landscape
papers.authors: Herbetko K, Herbetko A, Suwała S, Czarny J, Rudno-Rudzińska J, Milbrandt O
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains one of the most common malignancies worldwide and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Recent advances in CRC molecular biology have focused on biomarkers for early detection, prognostic stratification, treatment selection, and disease monitoring. Clinically validated biomarkers, including microsatellite instability (MSI), RAS and BRAF mutations, HER2 amplification, and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), guide targeted therapy and predict treatment response. However, tumor heterogeneity, clonal evolution, and microenvironmental influences limit the predictive value of single biomarkers. Recent molecular diagnostics therefore increasingly focus on dynamic and minimally invasive approaches. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is a promising biomarker for detecting minimal residual disease, monitoring recurrence, and assessing tumor evolution in real time. Multi-omics profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and artificial intelligence further expand tumor characterization except for conventional genomic alterations. Our review integrates common CRC biomarkers with developing liquid biopsy, multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, and artificial intelligence approaches across early detection, prognosis, treatment selection, and longitudinal monitoring. Future biomarker strategies will likely rely on integrated molecular models combined with longitudinal liquid-biopsy assessment. However, most new biomarkers remain at the investigational stage, and assay heterogeneity, limited standardization, and insufficient prospective clinical validation currently restrict their routine clinical use.

papers.title: Temperature as a Neglected Variable in Cancer: Cell-Intrinsic Thermal Sensitivity, Fever-Range Immunity, and the Febrile Paradox
papers.authors: Linnebacher M, Schwarz S, Schafmayer C
papers.abstract: Temperature is a fundamental physical variable affecting protein folding, proteostasis, cell-cycle kinetics, and immune function, yet cancer cell biology is performed almost exclusively at a fixed 37 °C, and distinct thermal phenomena are often conflated under the single term "hyperthermia." This review examines the biology of mild, fever-range temperature excursions of approximately 38-41 °C, which are mechanistically distinct from externally induced hyperthermia. We synthesize three strands of evidence that have rarely been considered together. First, tumor cells display heterogeneous thermal sensitivity, with differences in growth, cell-cycle responses, and thermal tolerance that may reflect intrinsic molecular features and proteostatic reserve, including the heat-shock response mediated by HSF1 and HSP70/HSP90. Second, fever-range temperatures remodel antitumor immunity across innate and adaptive compartments, affecting immune-cell trafficking, membrane organization, metabolism, and tumor-immune recognition. Third, the clinical record appears controversial: febrile infections have been associated with lower subsequent cancer risk, whereas postoperative fever has been associated with worse prognosis. We argue that these observations cannot be interpreted without considering host state, timing, and the biological context in which temperature elevation occurs. The three evidence streams are of unequal strength: cell-intrinsic thermal sensitivity and fever-range immune effects rest on direct experimental data, much of it from colorectal cancer, which we adopt as the principal proof-of-concept model, whereas the clinical associations are largely retrospective, and we treat them with correspondingly different confidence. We therefore frame a central testable question: is cell-intrinsic thermal sensitivity a cause or a correlate of fever's effects on cancer? We propose an experimental agenda that separates cell-autonomous thermal responses from host-mediated effects and establishes temperature as an explicit, biologically informative variable in cancer research.

papers.title: Zinc in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Biological Functions, Clinical Associations and Therapeutic Uncertainty
papers.authors: Hall R, Colwill M, Bancil A, Patel K, Honap S, Poullis A
papers.abstract: Zinc deficiency is reported in up to half of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), yet interpreting a low serum zinc concentration can be challenging. Zinc is an essential micronutrient with important roles in epithelial barrier integrity, immune regulation and cellular signalling, providing biological plausibility that deficiency could contribute to intestinal inflammation. Observational studies have associated low serum zinc with adverse outcomes, including hospitalisation, surgery and relapse, particularly in Crohn's disease. However, both systemic inflammation and hypoalbuminaemia reduce circulating zinc concentrations, raising uncertainty as to whether low zinc represents a true deficiency, a marker of active disease or a potentially modifiable contributor to inflammation. This narrative review examines the mechanistic, observational and interventional evidence linking zinc with IBD. Experimental studies support effects on tight-junction integrity, mucus production, Paneth cell function and immune signalling. Despite this biological rationale and the associations seen in observational studies, evidence that zinc supplementation improves IBD-related outcomes remains limited. Existing studies are small, heterogeneous and often rely on surrogate outcomes, while oral supplementation has not consistently improved clinical or inflammatory endpoints. Zinc deficiency should be identified and corrected as part of nutritional care in IBD but serum zinc concentrations should be interpreted in the context of underlying inflammation, and the benefit of routine zinc monitoring remains uncertain. Well-designed prospective trials are needed to determine whether correcting zinc deficiency improves objective IBD outcomes.

papers.title: Imatinib in the Treatment of Colorectal Cancer-Molecular Targets, Preclinical Evidence and Clinical Limitations
papers.authors: Wanke K, Kciuk M, Marciniak B, Kontek R
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major therapeutic challenge, despite substantial advances in molecular characterization and targeted treatment. The heterogeneity of CRC and the development of treatment resistance highlight the need for novel therapeutic strategies and rational drug repurposing approaches. Imatinib, a well-established tyrosine kinase inhibitor, exerts pharmacological activity beyond ABL1/ABL2, targeting KIT, PDGFR, DDR1, and potentially LCK, which may contribute to distinct mechanisms of CRC progression. This review examines the emerging evidence on the potential role of imatinib in CRC, including its effects on tumor-cell proliferation and survival, invasion and metastasis, extracellular-matrix remodeling, tumor-stroma interactions, treatment resistance, and immune regulation. Preclinical studies indicate promising antitumor activity in selected molecular and biological contexts, particularly in KIT-positive tumors, PDGFR-rich stroma, mesenchymal/CMS4 tumors, and models characterized by aberrant DDR1 signaling. However, clinical evidence remains limited and does not currently support imatinib as a standard treatment for unselected CRC. Biomarker-guided patient selection, rational combination strategies, and tumor microenvironment-directed approaches may enhance its therapeutic potential. Further well-designed clinical studies are required to determine whether these biological effects can translate into meaningful clinical benefit.

papers.title: Fecal Microbiota Transplantation in the Treatment Strategy of Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Molecular Mechanisms, Clinical Evidence, and the Transition Toward Defined Microbial Therapeutics
papers.authors: Pető A, Sipos D, Kappéter Á, Feiszt Z, Dembrovszky F, Halda-Kiss B
papers.abstract: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) comprises two clinically and pathologically distinct chronic intestinal inflammatory diseases, ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CD). Both diseases result from a dysregulated mucosal immune response to the commensal gut microbiota in genetically predisposed individuals. Because gut dysbiosis is a constant feature of both diseases, Fecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT) has recently been investigated as a potential therapeutic strategy to restore a balanced microbiota composition in patients with IBD. There are five placebo-controlled randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in UC and several meta-analyses, which showed that treatment with FMT using material from multiple donors can lead to clinical and endoscopic remission in patients with mild-to-moderate UC and may thus double to triple the rate of remission compared with placebo (number needed to treat [NNT] ≈ 3-5). In contrast, evidence for CD is limited and inconsistent, with one promising pilot study being contrasted with a large multicenter induction trial that was stopped for futility. This review provides an update of the current molecular understanding of FMT-induced recovery of mucosal barrier function and inflammation control in intestinal inflammation (α-diversity restoration and subsequent donor strain engraftment, production of short-chain fatty acids and secondary bile acids, tryptophan-AhR signaling, IL-10-mediated induction of Tregs vs. suppression of Th17 cells and restoration of epithelial barrier function). The review also summarizes the current clinical evidence for the use of FMT in IBD, its safety, and the current regulatory status. It also describes recent developments in FMT, including the use of defined bacterial consortia, 'live biotherapeutic products' (LBPs), and donor-recipient pairing. Collectively, FMT provides evidence of principle for manipulating intestinal microbial ecosystems to treat immune-mediated intestinal inflammation.

papers.title: Gut Microbiota as a Potential Modulator of Response to Biologic and Small-Molecule Therapies in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.abstract: The therapeutic landscape of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has expanded substantially with the development of biologic and small-molecule therapies. Nevertheless, many patients fail to respond to these treatments or experience a secondary loss of response. The mechanisms underlying treatment failure remain incompletely understood. Given the ability of gut microorganisms to modify therapeutic compounds, sustain pro-inflammatory immune activation, alter intestinal barrier function and produce bioactive metabolites, the gut microbiota may represent an important modulator of therapeutic response. To summarize current evidence on the role of the gut microbiota in response to biologic and small-molecule therapies in IBD, with particular emphasis on potential mechanisms of drug-microbiota interactions and their implications for treatment response and non-response. Accumulating evidence suggests that the gut microbiota may influence therapeutic efficacy through direct modification of drugs and indirect effects mediated by host immunity, intestinal barrier function and microbial metabolites. Microbial signatures associated with response to individual biologic therapies have been identified, although findings remain heterogeneous. Emerging evidence also indicates that non-bacterial components of the gut ecosystem may contribute to treatment response. The gut microbiota represents a biologically plausible modulator of therapeutic response in IBD. Integration of microbiome data with host genetic and immunological features may help identify biomarkers capable of predicting response to individual therapeutic agents.

papers.title: Short-Chain Fatty Acids as Modulators of the Gut-Immune Axis in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Linking Metabolism, Immune Regulation, and Epithelial Barrier Function
papers.authors: Piątek D, Sokal-Dembowska A, Strycharz-Dudziak M, Jarmakiewicz-Czaja S
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs), which include Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), are chronic conditions associated with abnormalities in the immune response, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and disruption of the intestinal barrier homeostasis. A growing body of evidence suggests that the gut-immune axis plays a key role in the pathogenesis of IBD, and that metabolites of microbial origin influence the regulation of the immune response and the maintenance of intestinal barrier integrity. Particular importance is attributed to short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate. The aim of this review is to present the current knowledge regarding the role of SCFAs as modulators of the gut-immune axis in IBD, with particular emphasis on their mechanisms of action and therapeutic potential. Physiologically, SCFAs are produced through the fermentation of dietary fiber by the gut microbiota. However, in IBD, the composition of the gut microbiota is often disrupted. SCFAs influence the expression of inflammatory genes and regulate the function of immune cells. Furthermore, butyrate in particular strengthens the integrity of the intestinal barrier by improving the function of tight junctions (TJs), increasing mucus production, and supporting epithelial regeneration. SCFAs represent an important link between diet, the gut microbiota, and immunity. Strategies to increase their availability may represent a promising approach to supporting IBD treatment, but they require further evaluation in well-designed clinical trials involving humans.

papers.title: Ceramides as Biomarkers of Risk Prediction and Prognosis in Cardiovascular and Other Diseases: Are We There Yet?
papers.authors: Garikipati T, Dubey P, Work D, Oli S, Sharma D, Chatterjee S
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide, yet roughly 70% of major adverse cardiovascular events occur in statin-treated patients with optimized Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), a gap that cholesterol-based risk panels do not close. Ceramides are bioactive sphingolipids whose plasma species and ratios carry risk information absent from standard lipid panels, and ceramide-based scores (CERT and CERT2) are already in clinical use. Whether this value extends beyond CVD is unclear. We reviewed ceramide species and ratios as biomarkers for disease prediction, prognosis, and disease activity across cardiovascular, metabolic, autoimmune rheumatic, inflammatory bowel, pulmonary, kidney, and oncologic contexts, searching PubMed and Scopus from January 1990 to June 2026 and extending the search for the historical literature. In CVD, CERT and CERT2 predicted cardiovascular events and mortality independently of LDL cholesterol, including in statin-treated and kidney disease populations. In metabolic and autoimmune rheumatic disease, ceramide profiles tracked cardiovascular risk and disease activity. In inflammatory bowel disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and most cancers, the evidence is mechanistically strong but limited to single-cohort or observational studies. Ceramides are emerging biomarkers that complement, not replace, established risk tools. Broader clinical use requires prospective validation, diverse cohorts, standardized assays, and demonstrated cost-effectiveness.
